$$

activity_context.topic_title: Cauchy-Euler Equations: Characteristic Equations With Repeated Roots

examples.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Involving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with a Repeated Root
examples.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
x^2 y'' - 19 xy' + 100y = 0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y =c_1 x^{10}+ c_2x ^{10}\ln x ,
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
x^2 y'' - 19 xy' + 100y = 0, \quad y(1) = 0,\quad  y'(1)=1, \quad x>0.
$$
examples.worked_solution:
We find the constants $c_1$ and $c_2$ using the initial conditions.

- First, we apply the condition $y(1)=0.$ Substituting $y(1)= 0$ into the general solution gives

$$
0= c_1.
$$

- Then, we apply the condition $y'(1) = 1.$ Differentiating $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =10{c}_{1}{x}^{9}+{c}_{2}{x}^{9}+10{c}_{2}{x}^{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y'(1)=1$ and $c_1 = 0$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =10{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ 1 & =0+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x) = x ^{10}\ln x .
$$

feedback.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
2{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+10t{y}^{′}+8y=0,\,t>0.
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}+10t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+8{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ 2\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }+10\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+8{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[2\lambda (\lambda -1)+10\lambda +8] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\lambda (\lambda -1)+10\lambda +8 & =0 \\ 2{\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +8 & =0 \\ 2({\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +4) & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have a double root $\lambda =-2.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}{t}^{-2}+{c}_{2}{t}^{-2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t.
$$
